**CR-4. Command anatomy, origin and intents.** A command is plain serializable data:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `type` | Registered command type ID, owned by a domain system |
| `issuer_peer` | Stamped by the kernel's ingress — never taken from the payload |
| `origin` | `PLAYER` or `SYSTEM`, stamped by ingress |
| `actor` | The entity the command acts as: an opaque ID in the ID space of the type's declared `actor_source` block (CR-7; IDs are block-local, CR-8, so one number can name different entities in two blocks), or none *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* |
| `seq` | Monotonically increasing integer per `(issuer_peer, origin)` — the host's `PLAYER` and `SYSTEM` streams are separate spaces *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. **Stamped by the kernel at ISSUED, never chosen by a local caller**: every local `INPUT_SURFACE` handle and `submit_system()` receives the next value of the one kernel-held counter for its `(issuer_peer, origin)`, so any number of surfaces sharing the `(1, PLAYER)` space can never collide; the counter advances on every submit, including one rejected at admission, so locally stamped values are dense (1, 2, 3 …) and `DUPLICATE_SEQ` and gap counting apply only to a `seq` supplied by the **test ingress or a remote ingress** (the only two callers that may supply one) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)* |
| `correlation` | Optional opaque `int` the submitting caller attaches (default 0 = none); the kernel never interprets it and echoes it unchanged in the command's result record and in any rejection event, so a caller (the Player Controller's pre-play tokens, a menu) matches a result to the act that caused it without learning or choosing `seq`. Kernel metadata like `submission_id`, never payload-borne; not part of `canonical_bytes` or any hash. Not unique: two submits may carry the same `correlation` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)* |
| `payload` | Plain data only, per the recursive whitelist below; no object references, node paths or callables; `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()` ≤ `MAX_PAYLOAD` |
| `queued_tick` | Stamped on enqueue |
| `submission_id` | Kernel metadata, never payload-borne: a kernel-unique counter stamped at ISSUED, before admission, so even a rejected submit has one; it is the `result_id` of the command's result (CR-5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |

*Discrete commands vs continuous intents.* If the sim must log, validate, save or replay it, it is a command (examples; each type's owner GDD is authoritative: Controller `set_move_intent`, `set_aim`, `toggle_beam`; Interaction `begin_cut` (module salvage, V8), `begin_patch`, `cancel_channel`, `pickup`, `drop`, `set_switch`, `field_check`; Modular Ship Assembly `begin_weld` (declared by Interaction, registered by Assembly), `begin_seam_cut`, `install_module` and the `SYSTEM`-only completions `weld` / `seam_cut` (registry: `assembly_commands`; there is no `remove_module` — it is reserved and unregistered, and V8 salvage is the only removal); Suit `equip_tool` (its only type); Web Map & Transit `pod_hop`, `berth`, `unberth` and the `SYSTEM`-only `pod_arrive`, `pod_settle`, `berth_step`, `web_reconcile` (registry: `web_commands`). `interact` is an input action, not a command type, and `use_item` has no owner and is not a command *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from interaction-system, suit-and-equipment, modular-ship-assembly and web-map-and-transit)*). What the stick is doing *right now* is an intent: intents are commands too, but a type may declare `coalesce = LATEST_PER_ACTOR_PER_TICK` — coalescing happens at admission over the unfrozen queue, keyed `(type, actor, issuer_peer)`, the older command becoming `Superseded` — and the input adapter sends one only when the quantised value changes — a few per second, never one per tick. Edge-triggered inputs (press, release, confirm) must declare `coalesce = NONE` or taps are lost. Movement integration runs inside the sim: Body's `body.integrate` hook (divisor 1, P3) reads the current intent and integrates ship-local kinematics (CR-13), so a move intent takes effect one tick after it is submitted, like every command; there is no physics-side integration at MVP, and position ownership is settled (Body owns it; the Controller owns intent and facing) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. Under `STRICT_DEBUG` every command is round-tripped through serialization before dispatch, even locally; one that cannot survive is a violation (CR-19). **Submit is fire-and-forget and never calls back**: `submit()` returns nothing and invokes no callback, handler or subscriber, so it is safe to call from any handler, hook or result handler; its only outcome is one result record appended to the kernel's result buffer (CR-5), delivered at the next flush and identified by `result_id` — a remote issuer could never get a synchronous answer, so the local one doesn't either *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. `submit()` takes the optional `correlation` and returns nothing, not even a receipt: the caller learns the outcome only from the result record, which carries its `correlation` back, so "fire-and-forget" is literally true and `seq` stays the kernel's. The API shape is `submit(type, payload, actor = none, correlation = 0)` on an `INPUT_SURFACE` handle and `submit_system(type, payload, dedupe_key = none)` for hooks (a hook needs no correlation: it never receives a result) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)*.

**Payload whitelist** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. 'Plain' is a recursive `Variant.Type` whitelist checked at admission: `NIL`, `BOOL`, `INT`, `FLOAT` (finite only — `NaN` and `±inf` are `MALFORMED`; the same finite check applies to **each component of a `VECTOR2` and each element of `PackedFloat32Array`, `PackedFloat64Array` and `PackedVector2Array`**, which the walk visits in O(n) bounded by `MAX_PAYLOAD` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*), `STRING`, `STRING_NAME`, `VECTOR2`, `VECTOR2I`, the `Packed{Byte,Int32,Int64,Float32,Float64,String,Vector2}Array` types, and `ARRAY`/`DICTIONARY` of the same, to a depth cap `PAYLOAD_MAX_DEPTH` = 8 (which also rejects a self-containing container). Dictionary keys must be `INT`, `STRING` or `STRING_NAME` and **all keys of one dictionary must share one type** (mixed keys have no canonical order, D.12). Anything else — an `Object`, `NodePath`, `Callable`, `Signal`, `RID`, a non-whitelisted `Variant.Type`, a non-finite float, a depth-9 nesting, mixed dictionary keys — is `MALFORMED`; the size bound is measured as `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()` after the walk passes. Immediate *acknowledgement* (a tool sound, a hand animation, a linear progress bar starting) is presentation's job and happens in the same frame; the sim confirms on the next tick. The latency bounds are stated once, in Game Feel and D.4.

**CR-5. Command lifecycle and the exactly-one-result guarantee.** Every command reaches exactly one terminal state and emits exactly one result record (identified by `result_id`; delivered to its issuer unless it is `SYSTEM`-origin, see Result identity and delivery below). Stages: *Issued* → *Admission* (kernel state accepts commands; type registered; **origin allowed for the type — known at admission, so rejected there**; queue not full; `seq` not a duplicate — gaps are accepted and counted, not rejected; issuer rate limit; payload plain) → *Queued* → *Authority check* in P2 (origin re-checked as a defence in depth; if the type declares `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER`, the binding table says the issuer controls the key `(actor_source, actor)` *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*; age ≤ the type's `max_age_ticks`) → *Validate* (owner's side-effect-free `validate(cmd, views, ctx)`: it reports through `ctx.ok()` or `ctx.reject(reason)` — a domain reason — and ends with `return ctx.complete()`; its return value carries no outcome, CR-19(a)/(b)) → *Apply* (`apply(cmd, write_scope, ctx)`, ending with `return ctx.complete()`; infallible by contract once validate passed, CR-9) → terminal: *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R3)*

| Terminal | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `Applied` | Effects are in state as of tick T (a command dispatched earlier in a tick that then faults is still `Applied`, with `detail.uncommitted = 1`) |
| `Rejected(reason)` | No effect |
| `Dropped(reason)` | Never evaluated: a reload, a shutdown or a fault flushed it — `RELOAD`, `SHUTDOWN`, `FAULTED` (the last added so G5 holds on the defect path). Includes the not-yet-dispatched commands of a faulting tick's batch *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |
| `Faulted(code)` | Evaluated, and its `validate` or `apply` (or a mutator it called) reported a fault through the fault channel (CR-19): effects may be partial and are unreachable to presentation. Exactly one command per fault — the cause. Distinct from `Rejected` (not 'no effect') and `Dropped` (not 'never evaluated') *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* |
| `Superseded` | Coalesced away by a newer command of a coalescing type |

Kernel reject reasons are a closed set: `NOT_ACCEPTING`, `PAUSED`, `UNKNOWN_TYPE`, `QUEUE_FULL`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `DUPLICATE_SEQ`, `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED`, `ACTOR_NOT_OWNED`, `STALE`, `MALFORMED`, `VALIDATION_FAILED(domain_code)` — domain codes are namespaced and owned by the registering system (Interaction's set, e.g. `OUT_OF_RANGE`, `INVALID_TARGET`, `PRECONDITION`, `BUSY`, is its GDD's). The result record carries `result_id`, `issuer_peer`, `origin`, `seq`, `correlation`, `ok`, `reason`, `subject` (the target the rejection refers to), an optional `detail` dictionary of numbers, and `tick` — **never display strings** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review: `result_id` and `origin` added)* *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2: `correlation` added, echoed unchanged from the submit)*. Presentation maps reasons to sound, shake or tooltip. **Reason codes are computed from true state and the kernel never filters them.** That is the whole of the kernel's claim. Whether, when and how cheaply a reason reaches the player is *not* the kernel's: Interaction, Sanity and the HUD own it and must obey Pillar 4's cost rule (a check costs time, risk or trust) — for example surfacing a `PRECONDITION` only after channel time has been spent, or only through diegetic feedback rather than an instant tooltip. *Design test (CD-GDD-ALIGN):* if a rejection lets the player falsify a hallucination at zero time, risk or trust cost, the presentation of that rejection is wrong — not the kernel. A command *aborted mid-channel* (power drops during a cut) is reported by the channel owner through state change, not through the command result. The kernel never retries.

**Result identity and delivery** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. A result is identified by `result_id` (the command's `submission_id`). A local issuer correlates by the `correlation` it attached to the submit (echoed unchanged; the caller's own uniqueness, not the kernel's), never by `seq`, which a local caller neither chooses nor learns *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R2)*. `(issuer_peer, origin, seq)` is unique among results **except** `DUPLICATE_SEQ` rejections, which by definition repeat an earlier command's `(issuer_peer, origin, seq)` and are told apart by `result_id` and `reason`; only a test or remote ingress can produce one (see the `seq` row of CR-4). Every terminal result — admission rejections, `Superseded`, P2 results, `Dropped(...)`, `Faulted` — is appended to the kernel's **result buffer** in the order it occurs; `submit()` itself never delivers. The buffer is flushed (a) at P5 of every tick, after the change batch, and (b) by the driver once per rendered frame after that frame's ticks, **in every kernel state** (`BOOTING`, `LOADING`, `PAUSED`, `SAVING`, `FAULTED`, `SHUTTING_DOWN`, and an idle frame with no tick), so `NOT_ACCEPTING`, `PAUSED`, `Dropped(RELOAD|SHUTDOWN|FAULTED)` and every other result always have a delivery point. A flush swaps the buffer out before delivering: whatever a result handler submits (the STALE resubmit of Section E, for example) is admitted normally, and any result it produces lands in the fresh buffer and is delivered at the next flush, never recursively — a handler that resubmits on every rejection costs one result per flush and cannot loop. Results go to the issuing `INPUT_SURFACE`'s result handler and to the diagnostics log. **`SYSTEM`-origin results are never delivered to a subscriber or to the submitting owner** (owners never subscribe, CR-10); they go to the command log and the diagnostics counters only, and an owner that needs the outcome reads state. **Fault semantics (a designer decision, not an implementer detail)**: when the kernel faults, each command already dispatched in the faulting tick whose `apply` completed receives `Applied` with `detail.uncommitted = 1` (its effects are in the live blocks although P4 never ran); the faulting command receives `Faulted(code)`; every not-yet-dispatched batch command and every pending command receives `Dropped(FAULTED)`; all are buffered at the fault transition and delivered at the next frame flush.

**CR-6. Registration at boot, then frozen.** Block, command-type, hook, diagnostics-channel and binding-source registration are legal only in `BOOTING` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from debug-overlay-true-values (E-DO-38))* (a block may declare one optional `binding_source` callable, CR-7; one registered after `BOOTING` is refused like every other registration *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*); after `BOOTING → LOADING` the registries are immutable until shutdown. Registration is an explicit declaration by the composition root, not discovery via the scene tree. Duplicate IDs, unknown types, missing owners and hook cycles fail boot loudly in every build. A command type registered without `allowed_origins`, `actor_binding`, `coalesce` or `max_age_ticks` (**no silent defaults**: an omitted `actor_binding` must never mean 'no ownership check'), a type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` but no `actor_source`, one whose `actor_source` names a block that registered no `binding_source`, and a `NONE` type that declares an `actor_source` (each fails boot with `ACTOR_SOURCE_INVALID`, naming the type) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*, a block registered without `class`, `gameplay`, `repl_hint` or `persist`, a type whose `writes_blocks` names an unregistered block, and an `allowed_when_paused` type whose `writes_blocks` names any `gameplay = true` block likewise fail boot (`BOOTING → FAULTED`) naming the registration. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `coalesce ≠ NONE` that allows both origins fails boot (`COALESCE_DUAL_ORIGIN`), because the supersession key carries no origin (D.8); and the joint memory assertion of Section G constraint 8 is checked here *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*.

**CR-7. Authority model (behaviour).** The host is the sole authority: only a `HOST` kernel ticks and applies; a `MIRROR` never applies. Each command type's owner declares `allowed_origins ⊆ {PLAYER, SYSTEM}` and `actor_binding ∈ {NONE, OWNED_BY_ISSUER}` — both mandatory (CR-6) — and `allowed_origins` is checked at admission, with a P2 re-check as defence in depth. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` also declares **`actor_source`**: the `block_id` of the registered binding source whose ID space its `actor` belongs to (`body.state` for every avatar-acting type, `emitter.state` for `toggle_beam`). The P2 authority check passes iff `(actor_source(type), actor) ∈ half_b[PlayerId(issuer_peer)]`. So an actor and a beam with the same number can never stand in for each other. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* `SYSTEM` commands never arrive from a network; remote ingress always stamps `PLAYER`. The kernel holds a **binding table** — `peer_id → PlayerId` and `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}` — as identity data, not domain state; the table has two halves with different lifetimes *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; Resolved 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling G6 (user delegated all remaining calls): the kernel owns the rebuild; closes Body Open Question 30)*. **(a) `peer_id → PlayerId`** is session state: it is mutated only through a host-only API called by the session owner (a boot step in MVP: `HOST_PEER_ID` 1 → PlayerId 1; Co-op Session in VS-B), and a restore, a death restart or a new game never touches it and never resets any issuer's `seq` or `last_seq`. **(b) `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}`** *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* is derived from saved state and is never saved: **the kernel rebuilds it itself as the last step of every pass through `LOADING`** (`request_restore` and `request_new_game` alike), after the last `post_restore()` and the K-4 hash check and before the `LOADING → RUNNING` transition. The rebuild clears half (b) entirely, then calls each registered **binding source** (CR-6, CR-8) in ascending `block_id` order — with `ctx`, as a pure read of its owner's block, under no `WriteScope`, ending `return ctx.complete()` — which delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` in ascending order through `ctx.put`, and binds every pair under the source's own `block_id`: each delivered `(player_id, entity_id)` is stored as `player_id → (source_block_id, entity_id)`. Entity IDs are block-local (CR-8: each owner allocates from its own counter and the kernel allocates none), so the key always carries the source. Equal numbers from two sources (Body actor 1 and Emitter beam 1) are two different keys and never conflict. A key `(source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered for two different PlayerIds, or the same triple `(player_id, source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered twice, is `BINDING_REBUILD_CONFLICT`. A source that reports `ctx.fault` or returns without the sentinel is that source's fault. Either one takes `LOADING → FAULTED` naming the source. The checks compare keys only within one source. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; registry request: `kernel_binding_table` `half_b`, `errors`, `actor_source`, `referenced_by`)* Because `LOADING` is atomic within one boundary service, the rebuild is not a P6 control-plane request and no command can interleave with it; the P6 rule (Section E) governs session-owner changes to half (a) only. At MVP no binding source's pairs change during `RUNNING`, so no `RUNNING` tick sees an empty or stale half (b); a runtime seat or beam reassignment (VS-B) is a session-owner request honoured at P6 (Open Question 4, the co-op ADR). MVP binding sources: Body's `seat_bindings()` (its `SEAT` rows → `(seat, actor_id)`) and the Emitter's `beam_bindings()` (`(player_id, beam_id)`). Single-player: PlayerId 1 → {(`body.state`, avatar actor_id), (`emitter.state`, beam_id)}. Both numbers may be 1 (two independent counters), and the result is valid. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix. Resolved 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix (G6): keyed by source rather than by namespace-tagged IDs, so Body's and the Emitter's persisted ID formats stay unchanged (G1).)* *(Alternative: Player Controller owns the binding as a block — rejected because the kernel could then not authority-check without calling a domain system. → ADR.)* **Single-player is not a special case**: local input is `PLAYER`-origin peer 1 (registry: `HOST_PEER_ID` = 1) acting on an entity peer 1 is bound to; the authority stage runs on every command from day one, so TD-FEASIBILITY's "authority discipline lapsing" risk is structural, not disciplinary. The kernel checks *who*; owners validate *whether the world allows it*; the kernel encodes no game rules. For friendly harm the kernel checks only issuer→actor ownership; the "attacker below the sanity threshold" gate is Interaction's `validate` calling Sanity's query on the actor's authoritative sanity level (a `SIM` block), never on anyone's perception.

**CR-15. Control plane** (host-local, not commands): `request_pause`, `request_resume`, `request_snapshot`, `request_restore`, `request_new_game` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review; CR-18)*, `request_shutdown`. Callers: Save/Load, the pause/Chart Table UI (host-local call), boot code. **Timing** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: a request is recorded when made — from any phase, from a hook, from a P5 handler, or from outside a tick (a UI call between frames) — and served at the **next boundary**, where a boundary is the P6 of a tick or the driver's per-frame boundary service (run before any tick of the frame and, while `PAUSED`, every frame), whichever comes first; the call itself never changes state. `request_shutdown` is accepted from **every state except `SHUTTING_DOWN`** (including `BOOTING`, `LOADING` and `SAVING`; in those it is served at the boundary that follows the atomic step). Requests reaching the same boundary are applied in arrival order, never coalesced: a `request_pause` then a `request_resume` on one boundary leaves the kernel `RUNNING` with no paused service cycle run; a caller that needs a definite state re-issues the state it wants (Chart Table CT-4) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from chart-table-web-map-and-menus (ASK-CT-9))*. **`request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash = none)`** (K-4) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R1; amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling R1 as amended by R13/R14: `restore_epoch` is supplied by Save/Load, whose epoch staging step has completed before the call is made: `EPOCH_DURABLE`, or a logged `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` with `save_status = FAILED`, or no advance was due. Save/Load advances the value on every death-stub restore, every `FAULT_RECOVERY` and every Continue except one of the newest non-demoted verified `QUIT` generation, which carries it unchanged and writes nothing (R13). The kernel never waits on that write: no Save/Load I/O completes inside `LOADING`, which stays atomic within one boundary service (States). **Listed exposure (failure path, R14):** after `SL_EPOCH_NOT_DURABLE` the installed epoch exists only in Save/Load's memory, so a process kill before Save/Load's next successful epoch write may replay that epoch once; G3/G4 are unaffected because they are defined given the `(save bytes, restore_epoch)` pair. The kernel holds it read-only for the session, exposes it in the `kernel.clock` read view (CR-8) and rejects a value outside the u32 range in its pre-check, `RESTORE_EPOCH_RANGE`)*: when an expected hash is given, the kernel recomputes `state_hash(PERSIST, T)` (D.12) after the last `post_restore()`, inside `LOADING` and before the first `RUNNING` tick, and reports `{T, computed_hash, match}` to the requester; Save/Load derives its EXACT / REBASED / mismatch verdict from it (SL-12). A mismatch is **not** a `FAULTED` transition — release plays on; policy is the requester's. Save/Load does not use restore-into-`PAUSED` for this window *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from save-load-and-versioned-format (K-4))*. **Control-plane read access:** a control-plane caller is not one of the CR-10 subscriber classes; Save/Load (the one such caller at MVP) may read `kernel.clock`, the Controller's per-seat `loco_state`, the Graph's `read_view.failures()` and an optional Attention `SIM` read view, and receives end-of-tick notifications, all read in the tick boundary in which it issues a request; it never reads `PERCEPTION_OUT`, never submits commands and never holds a `WriteScope` *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from save-load-and-versioned-format (SL-13))*. In VS-B a guest's pause or save *request* is a command defined by Session or Save/Load, validated on the host, which then calls the control API.

**CR-16. Pause semantics.** `PAUSED` stops the tick but not rendering. While paused, submit accepts only types flagged `allowed_when_paused` by their owner, and **only non-diegetic actions may carry the flag** (save, settings, resume, menu navigation) — no gameplay verb that changes `SIM` state is allowed while paused, so a solo player cannot equip, repair or re-route with time stopped mid-tell (Dread Before Chaos), and solo pause behaves like co-op's overlay-only pause; a paused-allowed command may write only blocks registered `gameplay = false` **and** named in the type's `writes_blocks` (boot-checked, CR-6; the `WriteScope` issued in the paused cycle carries exactly that set, and a write outside it is refused and counted as `WRITE_OUTSIDE_SCOPE`), never a `SIM` gameplay block *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; everything else is rejected `PAUSED` immediately, never queued, so there is no burst on resume. Admitted paused-allowed commands are dispatched by a **paused service cycle** that runs P1, P2, P4, P5 and P6 with no P3 and with `T` unchanged, **once per rendered frame while `PAUSED`** (the paused boundary, which also serves control-plane requests), so a save or a menu action takes effect without advancing simulated time. At MVP no command type sets the flag; the cycle is a retained seam that only test fixtures exercise (CR-2). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Commands already queued when the pause is honoured are neither dispatched by the service cycle nor rejected: they wait, in order, for the first `RUNNING` tick after resume. **Pause is single-player only**: in co-op a menu cannot stop a shared sim — VS-B treats pause as a UI overlay with the kernel `RUNNING`. The Chart Table GDD must not assume "pick a target" happens while paused. Relationship to the scene tree's pause → ADR.

**CR-17. Bounds and overload behaviour.** At most `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK` processed per tick, the rest waiting FIFO. `QUEUE_CAPACITY` total and `PER_ISSUER_CAPACITY` per issuer; beyond that `QUEUE_FULL` at admission — never silent drop, never unbounded growth. Catch-up runs at most `MAX_TICKS_PER_FRAME` ticks per frame, then lets simulated time lag rather than spiral (lag above `LAG_FORGIVE_TICKS` is dropped at the end of the frame, D.5); a lag counter is exposed to diagnostics. P3 exceeding `STEP_BUDGET_MS` logs the slowest hooks but the tick completes. A command older than its type's `max_age_ticks` is rejected `STALE`, so a hitch cannot unleash a second of stale intents. At the defaults `STALE` is unreachable from local ingress (the queue can hold a command at most 8 ticks and `T` does not advance while paused or saving); it is a VS-B seam for remote-stamped ticks, guarded locally by a "never stale" invariant test (Section E; ratified 2026-10-27 — user ruling, R-3). *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)*
======
## Decision

### 1. Capability handles are the only way in

There is no global `submit`. The composition root (ADR-0001) holds the kernel in `BOOTING` and issues two kinds of handle, each by name, each once:

83	### 2. One ingress function stamps every command
84	
85	All paths (surface handle, `submit_system`, the future remote ingress, the test ingress) call one kernel-private function:
86	
87	```gdscript
88	func _admit(origin: int, issuer_peer: int, type: StringName, payload: Dictionary,
89			actor: int, correlation: int, supplied_seq: int) -> void   # supplied_seq only from the test or remote ingress
90	```
91	
92	It performs, in order: stamp `submission_id` (a kernel-unique counter, so even a rejected submit has one) → stamp `seq` from the one kernel-held counter for `(issuer_peer, origin)` unless the test or remote ingress supplied one → resolve the type (`UNKNOWN_TYPE`) → check kernel state (`NOT_ACCEPTING`; `PAUSED` unless the type is `allowed_when_paused`) → origin allowed for the type (`ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED`) → duplicate `seq` (`DUPLICATE_SEQ`, test and remote only) → rate limit (`RATE_LIMITED`, remote only) → payload walk, size and schema (`MALFORMED`) → coalescing (§ 5) → queue capacity (`QUEUE_FULL`) → enqueue with `queued_tick` = current `T`. 93	
94	`Command` is a `RefCounted` record with typed fields (`type_idx`, `issuer_peer`, `origin`, `actor`, `seq`, `correlation`, `payload`, `queued_tick`, `submission_id`, `host_order`) plus two kernel-only fields, `_sealed` and `_slot` (the `submission_id` it was admitted under). **Only `_admit` fills it, and only the queue owns the instances.** GDScript cannot make a constructor private, so the rule is enforced twice: at run time, `_admit` sets `_sealed = true` after filling a `Command` and records its `submission_id` in `_slot`, and the dispatch path (P1, P2, apply) refuses any `Command` that is unsealed or whose `_slot` does not match the queue entry it came from; and a CI check greps for `Command.new()` outside `src/kernel/`. `Command` has no `_init` parameter for `issuer_peer` at all. This is the "no constructor without `issuer_peer` exists" rule (kernel H6) in a form GDScript can state.
95	
96	**No object is reused.** The ring holds references to `Command` instances; each admitted submit allocates one (a few tens per second, negligible, and the same order as the `var_to_bytes` allocation the size check already accepts); a slot is released by assigning `null`. Nothing pools or recycles a `Command`, so no `validate`, `apply`, result record or log entry can see a reused object. Even so, **owners must not retain `cmd` past the callable it was passed to** (copy the scalar fields needed), and **result and log records copy the scalar fields they need rather than holding a `Command`**. The command log copies the payload bytes.
97	
98	Command types are addressed by `StringName` in the call and resolved once to a small integer `type_idx` at registration; the hot path is one `Dictionary` lookup keyed by `StringName`.
99	
100	### 3. Payload schema per command type, enforced at admission
101	
102	The kernel GDD checks payloads against a recursive `Variant.Type` whitelist (finite floats, depth ≤ 8, uniform dictionary key type, size ≤ 4 KiB via `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()`). 103	
104	```gdscript
105	# Keys are the payload dictionary keys; values describe the expected value.
106	payload_schema = {
107		&"target": {&"type": TYPE_INT, &"required": true},
108		&"face_octant": {&"type": TYPE_INT, &"required": false, &"min": 0, &"max": 8},
109	}
110	```
111

Packed arrays are whitelisted and counted in the byte estimate (a large `PackedByteArray` passes the type check but not the budget). The range checks in step 3 test `is_finite()` first, because `NAN < min` and `NAN > max` are both false and a naive range test would pass `NAN`.
113	
114	Admission checks, after the whitelist walk passes: every required key present; no key outside the schema; each value of the declared `Variant.Type` (an `int` where `float` is declared is `MALFORMED`, never silently converted); integers and floats inside the declared inclusive range when one is given. Ids above 2^53 must never pass through JSON (a JSON number parses as a float and loses precision); saves carry them as packed integer arrays (ADR-0006). A mismatch is `MALFORMED`. A type with no payload registers an explicit empty schema `{}` (no silent default, matching CR-6's rule for the other mandatory fields); omitting the field fails boot.
115	
116	The schema is data on the descriptor, so the same table drives the admission check, the STRICT_DEBUG serialisation round-trip test, the control-manifest's list of commands, and the debug overlay's command panel.
117	
118	### 4. Ownership is a kernel binding table keyed by PlayerId
119	
120	Exactly as CR-7: half (a) `peer_id → PlayerId` is session state set by a host-only API (a boot step in the MVP: `HOST_PEER_ID` 1 → PlayerId 1), never touched by a restore, new game or death restart, and never resetting any issuer's `seq`. The data structure:
121	
122	- Half (a): a `Dictionary` `int → int`.
123	- Half (b): per PlayerId, one small `PlayerBindings` object holding two parallel `PackedInt64Array`s (source block index, entity id) behind one `add` / `remove` / `owns(source, entity)` interface, so the arrays cannot drift out of step. A player owns a handful of entities (an avatar and a beam), so `owns` is a linear scan of a few elements with no composite-key hashing and no allocation. Mutation is an explicit read-modify-write on the object's own arrays (never `dict[k].append(x)` on a packed array stored in a dictionary, whose behaviour has varied across versions), covered by a unit test.
124	- **Determinism of iteration.** The `LOADING` rebuild and every registry walk iterate **sorted** arrays (block ids ascending, command types in registration order recorded in an array), never `keys()` of a Dictionary filled from an unordered source. Dictionaries preserve insertion order in Godot 4, but erasing and re-inserting a key moves it to the end, so no hash or rebuild may depend on it.
125	
126	A command type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` passes P2 iff `(actor_source(type), actor)` is in half (b) of `PlayerId(issuer_peer)`; otherwise it is `Rejected(ACTOR_NOT_OWNED)` with no state change. Persistent state is keyed by PlayerId; the peer id appears only in the ingress stamp and the binding table. Ownership is **never** derived from scene-tree node ownership, `set_multiplayer_authority()` or any engine multiplayer primitive.
127	
128	### 5. Ordering, coalescing and the queue
129	
130	- Apply order is ascending `(queued_tick, host_order)`, where `host_order` is the arrival counter at `_admit`; in single-player it is submission order (CR-13 G1).
131	- The queue is one preallocated ring of `Command` slots sized to `QUEUE_CAPACITY` with per-issuer counters for `PER_ISSUER_CAPACITY` and a `SYSTEM_RESERVE` so SYSTEM commands cannot be starved by a flood of PLAYER ones. Overflow is `QUEUE_FULL` at admission, never a silent drop. **Accounting rule:** the capacity counters (`QUEUE_CAPACITY`, `PER_ISSUER_CAPACITY`) decrement the moment a command is superseded, P1 skips tombstones and counts only live commands against `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK`, and the tombstone's ring position is reclaimed when the head passes it, so an aim stream under backlog cannot cause a spurious `QUEUE_FULL`. On entry to `LOADING`, `SHUTTING_DOWN` or `FAULTED` the queue is flushed and every queued command receives `Dropped(RELOAD|SHUTDOWN|FAULTED)` (the exactly-one-result guarantee, CR-5 and G5).
132	- **Coalescing** (`coalesce = LATEST_PER_ACTOR_PER_TICK`) is done by scanning the unfrozen portion of the queue for a command with the same `(type_idx, actor, issuer_peer)` and marking the older one `Superseded`. The scan runs only when a coalescing type is submitted, and intent types are sent a few times per second (aim at most every 3 ticks), so the scan over at most 1,024 slots is cheap and avoids a second index structure that would have to be kept in step with the ring. A type with `coalesce ≠ NONE` that allows both origins fails boot (`COALESCE_DUAL_ORIGIN`).
133	- Each tick, P1 moves at most `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK` commands into the frozen batch for P2; the rest wait FIFO.
134	- A command older than its type's `max_age_ticks` is `STALE`. At local defaults this is unreachable (CR-17) and is guarded by an invariant test.
135	
136	### 6. The control plane is a host-local API on a `ControlHandle`
137	
138	`request_pause()`, `request_resume()`, `request_snapshot()`, `request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash)`, `request_new_game(world_seed, restore_epoch)`, `request_shutdown()`, `request_bind_seat(peer_id, player_id)` and `request_unbind_seat(peer_id)` are methods of `ControlHandle`, not commands. They are not stamped, queued, authority-checked or logged as commands. Each call is appended to a small host-local request list and served **at the next boundary service, in arrival order** (ADR-0001 § 1), and each request ends in exactly one outcome: `SERVED`, `DEFERRED` (made while an atomic step was active; evaluated at the first boundary after it) or `IGNORED` (a (state, trigger) pair the transition table does not list; one invalid-transition entry, no state change). **Outcome delivery.** Outcomes are always recorded in diagnostics. Callers that must act on one set `ControlHandle.set_outcome_handler(Callable)` and receive a typed `ControlOutcome` (`request_kind`, `outcome`, `tick`, and for `request_restore` the K-4 verdict `{T, computed_hash, match}`; for `request_snapshot` the captured payload, a deep copy) at the same per-frame flush point as command results, **in a separate list that is never part of the CR-5 command result buffer**. This amends one sentence of the kernel GDD (States and Transitions, "control-plane requests have none"; § GDD sync): the outcome list is not a command result record, but it exists, because Save/Load needs the snapshot payload and the K-4 verdict (CR-15) and PauseGate needs to converge. Two consequences are intentional: a `request_pause` and a `request_resume` in the same boundary pair up in order, and `PauseGate` (Chart Table) re-issues the latest desired pause state until the kernel matches it, so a same-boundary pair leaves no wedged half-open state (TR-charttable-004).
139	
140	**Seat binding (binding table half (a)).** `request_bind_seat(peer_id, player_id)` and `request_unbind_seat(peer_id)` are the host-only writers of `peer_id → PlayerId` (CR-7). The composition root, holding the `game` control handle, calls `request_bind_seat(HOST_PEER_ID, 1)` as its boot step; the Co-op Session calls the same two methods in VS-B, so the kernel's public API does not widen then. A restore, new game or death restart never touches half (a). Runtime seat reassignment (kernel open question 4) is deferred to ADR-0032 under this signature. When `issuer_peer` has no half (a) entry, a type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` is `Rejected(ACTOR_NOT_OWNED)`; a `NONE` type proceeds.
141	
142	Pause is single-player only. While `PAUSED` the kernel accepts only command types flagged `allowed_when_paused` whose `writes_blocks` name no `gameplay = true` block; everything else is rejected `PAUSED` at admission without queuing (CR-16). The control plane is host-local by construction: a remote ingress has no `ControlHandle`.
143	
144	This ADR owns how requests are accepted, ordered and answered. The states they move between (`RUNNING`, `PAUSED`, `SAVING`, `LOADING`, `FAULTED`, `SHUTTING_DOWN`) and the transitions' internals belong to ADR-0003.
145	
146	### 7. Result delivery
147	
148	Results are plain records (`result_id`, `issuer_peer`, `origin`, `seq`, `correlation`, `ok`, `reason`, `subject`, `detail`, `tick`) appended to the kernel's result buffer and flushed at P5 and once per rendered frame in every kernel state. A flush swaps the buffer out before delivering, so a handler that resubmits cannot recurse; it iterates that local array and re-checks each handler's validity per item, so a handler that frees its owner or its surface mid-flush invalidates only itself. `issue_surface_handle` and `issue_control_handle` are legal only in `BOOTING`, so a handler calling them mid-flush is a violation (CR-19), not a new handle. PLAYER results go to the issuing `SurfaceHandle`'s result handler and to the diagnostics log. SYSTEM results go to the command log and diagnostics counters only; an owner that needs an outcome reads state. Reason codes are computed from true state and never filtered by the kernel; whether and how cheaply a reason reaches the player is the presenter's rule (Pillar 4 cost rule), not this pipeline's.
149	
150	### 8. HOST and MIRROR share one API; ingress is the only difference
151	
152	On a MIRROR kernel `SurfaceHandle.submit` routes to an egress adapter (VS-B, ADR-0032), not to `_admit`; the handle's API is unchanged. `Kernel` is constructed with `Mode.HOST` or `Mode.MIRROR` and a `KernelProfile` (`STRICT_DEBUG` or `LENIENT_RELEASE`, injected, never read from `OS.is_debug_build()`). The public API is identical. A MIRROR does not tick and does not apply; it exists in the MVP only as a mode flag with a unit test proving `step()` refuses to apply in that mode. The ingress kinds are:
153	
154	| Ingress | Origin it stamps | `issuer_peer` | May supply `seq` | Exists in |
155	|---|---|---|---|---|
156	| Local surface handle | PLAYER | the handle's peer (`HOST_PEER_ID` = 1) | no | MVP |
157	| `submit_system` on a context | SYSTEM | `HOST_PEER_ID` | no | MVP |
158	| Test ingress | either | caller's choice | yes | tests only: lives under `tests/`, is injected by the harness, and is never named by a `class_name` that shipped code references (an export filter removes files, and a referenced missing class fails to load) |
159	| Remote ingress adapter | PLAYER, always (it has no origin parameter) | the network sender id, read only here | yes | VS-B (ADR-0032) |
160	
161	The remote ingress adapter is the only place in the project that reads a network sender id, and `SYSTEM` commands never arrive from a network by construction: the adapter cannot stamp that origin.

```gdscript
		actor: int, correlation: int, supplied_seq: int) -> void   # supplied_seq only from the test or remote ingress
```

It performs, in order: stamp `submission_id` (a kernel-unique counter, so even a rejected submit has one) → stamp `seq` from the one kernel-held counter for `(issuer_peer, origin)` unless the test or remote ingress supplied one → resolve the type (`UNKNOWN_TYPE`) → check kernel state (`NOT_ACCEPTING`; `PAUSED` unless the type is `allowed_when_paused`) → origin allowed for the type (`ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED`) → duplicate `seq` (`DUPLICATE_SEQ`, test and remote only) → rate limit (`RATE_LIMITED`, remote only) → payload walk, size and schema (`MALFORMED`) → coalescing (§ 5) → queue capacity (`QUEUE_FULL`) → enqueue with `queued_tick` = current `T`. Any rejection appends one result record and returns; nothing is thrown. The counter advances on every submit including rejected ones, so locally stamped values are dense (CR-4). **This order is normative** and goes into the kernel GDD (§ GDD sync) so tests are written against one order. It differs from CR-5's prose in one observable way: the type is resolved before the kernel-state check, because the `allowed_when_paused` exemption (CR-16) needs the type, so an unknown type submitted while `PAUSED` is `UNKNOWN_TYPE`, not `PAUSED`. The capacity check comes after coalescing because a supersession can free room.

`Command` is a `RefCounted` record with typed fields (`type_idx`, `issuer_peer`, `origin`, `actor`, `seq`, `correlation`, `payload`, `queued_tick`, `submission_id`, `host_order`) plus two kernel-only fields, `_sealed` and `_slot` (the `submission_id` it was admitted under). **Only `_admit` fills it, and only the queue owns the instances.** GDScript cannot make a constructor private, so the rule is enforced twice: at run time, `_admit` sets `_sealed = true` after filling a `Command` and records its `submission_id` in `_slot`, and the dispatch path (P1, P2, apply) refuses any `Command` that is unsealed or whose `_slot` does not match the queue entry it came from; and a CI check greps for `Command.new()` outside `src/kernel/`. `Command` has no `_init` parameter for `issuer_peer` at all. This is the "no constructor without `issuer_peer` exists" rule (kernel H6) in a form GDScript can state.

**No object is reused.** The ring holds references to `Command` instances; each admitted submit allocates one (a few tens per second, negligible, and the same order as the `var_to_bytes` allocation the size check already accepts); a slot is released by assigning `null`. Nothing pools or recycles a `Command`, so no `validate`, `apply`, result record or log entry can see a reused object. Even so, **owners must not retain `cmd` past the callable it was passed to** (copy the scalar fields needed), and **result and log records copy the scalar fields they need rather than holding a `Command`**. The command log copies the payload bytes.

Command types are addressed by `StringName` in the call and resolved once to a small integer `type_idx` at registration; the hot path is one `Dictionary` lookup keyed by `StringName`.

### 3. Payload schema per command type, enforced at admission

The kernel GDD checks payloads against a recursive `Variant.Type` whitelist (finite floats, depth ≤ 8, uniform dictionary key type, size ≤ 4 KiB via `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size()`). That says what a payload may be made of, not what a given command carries. This ADR adds a **mandatory `payload_schema`** to the command-type descriptor:

```gdscript
# Keys are the payload dictionary keys; values describe the expected value.
payload_schema = {
	&"target": {&"type": TYPE_INT, &"required": true},
	&"face_octant": {&"type": TYPE_INT, &"required": false, &"min": 0, &"max": 8},
}
```

**Order of the payload checks.** (1) The whitelist walk: `typeof()` against a constant set of allowed `Variant.Type`s, every dictionary key a `StringName` for payload dictionaries (a `String` key is `MALFORMED`, so the schema lookup is exact), all keys of any nested dictionary of one type, depth cap `PAYLOAD_MAX_DEPTH` 8, `is_finite()` on every float and on every component of `Vector2` and each element of the float and `Vector2` packed arrays, and a running upper-bound byte estimate that aborts the walk the moment it exceeds `MAX_PAYLOAD`. (2) Only after the walk passes, `var_to_bytes(payload, false).size() <= MAX_PAYLOAD`. (3) The schema below. A cyclic container is rejected by the depth cap at step 1, never serialised. Packed arrays are whitelisted and counted in the byte estimate (a large `PackedByteArray` passes the type check but not the budget). The range checks in step 3 test `is_finite()` first, because `NAN < min` and `NAN > max` are both false and a naive range test would pass `NAN`.

Admission checks, after the whitelist walk passes: every required key present; no key outside the schema; each value of the declared `Variant.Type` (an `int` where `float` is declared is `MALFORMED`, never silently converted); integers and floats inside the declared inclusive range when one is given. Entity and actor ids are `int` (64-bit in GDScript) and are non-negative; `NO_ACTOR` is `-1`, which no real id can equal. Ids above 2^53 must never pass through JSON (a JSON number parses as a float and loses precision); saves carry them as packed integer arrays (ADR-0006). A mismatch is `MALFORMED`. The dictionary form above is authoring syntax. At registration the kernel **compiles each schema into parallel arrays** (keys, types, required flags, bounds) and validates it at boot: an unknown schema key (a typo such as `&"minn"`) fails boot, and a bound whose type does not match the field's declared type fails boot (an `int` field with a `float` bound would otherwise compare silently). Admission then walks the compiled arrays, not nested dictionaries. The schema is **flat**: it covers the top-level keys of the payload. Nested `ARRAY`, `DICTIONARY` and packed values are checked **by type only** (the whitelist walk already checked element types, depth and key-type uniformity), and what their elements mean stays in the owner's `validate`; a later `elements` sub-schema is possible but not needed by the MVP commands (SYSTEM payloads such as `weld {actor, target, cause}` are flat). Payload dictionaries use `StringName` keys; a caller that writes `{"target": x}` produces a `String` key and is `MALFORMED`, so no lookup depends on `String`/`StringName` equivalence. The schema describes **shape only**; whether the target exists, is in reach or is lit stays in the owner's `validate`, so a rejection reason is never produced by the schema layer except `MALFORMED`. A type with no payload registers an explicit empty schema `{}` (no silent default, matching CR-6's rule for the other mandatory fields); omitting the field fails boot.

The schema is data on the descriptor, so the same table drives the admission check, the STRICT_DEBUG serialisation round-trip test, the control-manifest's list of commands, and the debug overlay's command panel.

### 4. Ownership is a kernel binding table keyed by PlayerId

Exactly as CR-7: half (a) `peer_id → PlayerId` is session state set by a host-only API (a boot step in the MVP: `HOST_PEER_ID` 1 → PlayerId 1), never touched by a restore, new game or death restart, and never resetting any issuer's `seq`. Half (b) `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}` is derived from saved state and is never saved; the kernel rebuilds it as the last step of every pass through `LOADING` from the registered binding sources in ascending `block_id` order. The data structure:

- Half (a): a `Dictionary` `int → int`.
- Half (b): per PlayerId, one small `PlayerBindings` object holding two parallel `PackedInt64Array`s (source block index, entity id) behind one `add` / `remove` / `owns(source, entity)` interface, so the arrays cannot drift out of step. A player owns a handful of entities (an avatar and a beam), so `owns` is a linear scan of a few elements with no composite-key hashing and no allocation. Mutation is an explicit read-modify-write on the object's own arrays (never `dict[k].append(x)` on a packed array stored in a dictionary, whose behaviour has varied across versions), covered by a unit test.
- **Determinism of iteration.** The `LOADING` rebuild and every registry walk iterate **sorted** arrays (block ids ascending, command types in registration order recorded in an array), never `keys()` of a Dictionary filled from an unordered source. Dictionaries preserve insertion order in Godot 4, but erasing and re-inserting a key moves it to the end, so no hash or rebuild may depend on it.

A command type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` passes P2 iff `(actor_source(type), actor)` is in half (b) of `PlayerId(issuer_peer)`; otherwise it is `Rejected(ACTOR_NOT_OWNED)` with no state change. Persistent state is keyed by PlayerId; the peer id appears only in the ingress stamp and the binding table. Ownership is **never** derived from scene-tree node ownership, `set_multiplayer_authority()` or any engine multiplayer primitive.

### 5. Ordering, coalescing and the queue

- Apply order is ascending `(queued_tick, host_order)`, where `host_order` is the arrival counter at `_admit`; in single-player it is submission order (CR-13 G1).
- The queue is one preallocated ring of `Command` slots sized to `QUEUE_CAPACITY` with per-issuer counters for `PER_ISSUER_CAPACITY` and a `SYSTEM_RESERVE` so SYSTEM commands cannot be starved by a flood of PLAYER ones. Overflow is `QUEUE_FULL` at admission, never a silent drop. **Accounting rule:** the capacity counters (`QUEUE_CAPACITY`, `PER_ISSUER_CAPACITY`) decrement the moment a command is superseded, P1 skips tombstones and counts only live commands against `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK`, and the tombstone's ring position is reclaimed when the head passes it, so an aim stream under backlog cannot cause a spurious `QUEUE_FULL`. On entry to `LOADING`, `SHUTTING_DOWN` or `FAULTED` the queue is flushed and every queued command receives `Dropped(RELOAD|SHUTDOWN|FAULTED)` (the exactly-one-result guarantee, CR-5 and G5).
- **Coalescing** (`coalesce = LATEST_PER_ACTOR_PER_TICK`) is done by scanning the unfrozen portion of the queue for a command with the same `(type_idx, actor, issuer_peer)` and marking the older one `Superseded`. The scan runs only when a coalescing type is submitted, and intent types are sent a few times per second (aim at most every 3 ticks), so the scan over at most 1,024 slots is cheap and avoids a second index structure that would have to be kept in step with the ring. A type with `coalesce ≠ NONE` that allows both origins fails boot (`COALESCE_DUAL_ORIGIN`).
- Each tick, P1 moves at most `MAX_CMDS_PER_TICK` commands into the frozen batch for P2; the rest wait FIFO.
- A command older than its type's `max_age_ticks` is `STALE`. At local defaults this is unreachable (CR-17) and is guarded by an invariant test.

### 6. The control plane is a host-local API on a `ControlHandle`

`request_pause()`, `request_resume()`, `request_snapshot()`, `request_restore(payload, restore_epoch, expected_state_hash)`, `request_new_game(world_seed, restore_epoch)`, `request_shutdown()`, `request_bind_seat(peer_id, player_id)` and `request_unbind_seat(peer_id)` are methods of `ControlHandle`, not commands. They are not stamped, queued, authority-checked or logged as commands. Each call is appended to a small host-local request list and served **at the next boundary service, in arrival order** (ADR-0001 § 1), and each request ends in exactly one outcome: `SERVED`, `DEFERRED` (made while an atomic step was active; evaluated at the first boundary after it) or `IGNORED` (a (state, trigger) pair the transition table does not list; one invalid-transition entry, no state change). **Outcome delivery.** Outcomes are always recorded in diagnostics. Callers that must act on one set `ControlHandle.set_outcome_handler(Callable)` and receive a typed `ControlOutcome` (`request_kind`, `outcome`, `tick`, and for `request_restore` the K-4 verdict `{T, computed_hash, match}`; for `request_snapshot` the captured payload, a deep copy) at the same per-frame flush point as command results, **in a separate list that is never part of the CR-5 command result buffer**. This amends one sentence of the kernel GDD (States and Transitions, "control-plane requests have none"; § GDD sync): the outcome list is not a command result record, but it exists, because Save/Load needs the snapshot payload and the K-4 verdict (CR-15) and PauseGate needs to converge. Two consequences are intentional: a `request_pause` and a `request_resume` in the same boundary pair up in order, and `PauseGate` (Chart Table) re-issues the latest desired pause state until the kernel matches it, so a same-boundary pair leaves no wedged half-open state (TR-charttable-004).

**Seat binding (binding table half (a)).** `request_bind_seat(peer_id, player_id)` and `request_unbind_seat(peer_id)` are the host-only writers of `peer_id → PlayerId` (CR-7). The composition root, holding the `game` control handle, calls `request_bind_seat(HOST_PEER_ID, 1)` as its boot step; the Co-op Session calls the same two methods in VS-B, so the kernel's public API does not widen then. A restore, new game or death restart never touches half (a). Runtime seat reassignment (kernel open question 4) is deferred to ADR-0032 under this signature. When `issuer_peer` has no half (a) entry, a type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` is `Rejected(ACTOR_NOT_OWNED)`; a `NONE` type proceeds.

Pause is single-player only. While `PAUSED` the kernel accepts only command types flagged `allowed_when_paused` whose `writes_blocks` name no `gameplay = true` block; everything else is rejected `PAUSED` at admission without queuing (CR-16). The control plane is host-local by construction: a remote ingress has no `ControlHandle`.

This ADR owns how requests are accepted, ordered and answered. The states they move between (`RUNNING`, `PAUSED`, `SAVING`, `LOADING`, `FAULTED`, `SHUTTING_DOWN`) and the transitions' internals belong to ADR-0003.

### 7. Result delivery

Results are plain records (`result_id`, `issuer_peer`, `origin`, `seq`, `correlation`, `ok`, `reason`, `subject`, `detail`, `tick`) appended to the kernel's result buffer and flushed at P5 and once per rendered frame in every kernel state. A flush swaps the buffer out before delivering, so a handler that resubmits cannot recurse; it iterates that local array and re-checks each handler's validity per item, so a handler that frees its owner or its surface mid-flush invalidates only itself. `issue_surface_handle` and `issue_control_handle` are legal only in `BOOTING`, so a handler calling them mid-flush is a violation (CR-19), not a new handle. PLAYER results go to the issuing `SurfaceHandle`'s result handler and to the diagnostics log. SYSTEM results go to the command log and diagnostics counters only; an owner that needs an outcome reads state. Reason codes are computed from true state and never filtered by the kernel; whether and how cheaply a reason reaches the player is the presenter's rule (Pillar 4 cost rule), not this pipeline's.

### 8. HOST and MIRROR share one API; ingress is the only difference

On a MIRROR kernel `SurfaceHandle.submit` routes to an egress adapter (VS-B, ADR-0032), not to `_admit`; the handle's API is unchanged. `Kernel` is constructed with `Mode.HOST` or `Mode.MIRROR` and a `KernelProfile` (`STRICT_DEBUG` or `LENIENT_RELEASE`, injected, never read from `OS.is_debug_build()`). The public API is identical. A MIRROR does not tick and does not apply; it exists in the MVP only as a mode flag with a unit test proving `step()` refuses to apply in that mode. The ingress kinds are:

| Ingress | Origin it stamps | `issuer_peer` | May supply `seq` | Exists in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Local surface handle | PLAYER | the handle's peer (`HOST_PEER_ID` = 1) | no | MVP |
| `submit_system` on a context | SYSTEM | `HOST_PEER_ID` | no | MVP |
| Test ingress | either | caller's choice | yes | tests only: lives under `tests/`, is injected by the harness, and is never named by a `class_name` that shipped code references (an export filter removes files, and a referenced missing class fails to load) |
| Remote ingress adapter | PLAYER, always (it has no origin parameter) | the network sender id, read only here | yes | VS-B (ADR-0032) |

The remote ingress adapter is the only place in the project that reads a network sender id, and `SYSTEM` commands never arrive from a network by construction: the adapter cannot stamp that origin.

**CR-16. Pause semantics.** `PAUSED` stops the tick but not rendering. While paused, submit accepts only types flagged `allowed_when_paused` by their owner, and **only non-diegetic actions may carry the flag** (save, settings, resume, menu navigation) — no gameplay verb that changes `SIM` state is allowed while paused, so a solo player cannot equip, repair or re-route with time stopped mid-tell (Dread Before Chaos), and solo pause behaves like co-op's overlay-only pause; a paused-allowed command may write only blocks registered `gameplay = false` **and** named in the type's `writes_blocks` (boot-checked, CR-6; the `WriteScope` issued in the paused cycle carries exactly that set, and a write outside it is refused and counted as `WRITE_OUTSIDE_SCOPE`), never a `SIM` gameplay block *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; everything else is rejected `PAUSED` immediately, never queued, so there is no burst on resume. Every other `(state, trigger)` pair is invalid: the kernel ignores it and reports it to diagnostics, never silently changing state. No transition leaves `SAVING` except to its return state or `FAULTED`; a restore requested while `SAVING` is active is queued and served after the capture (the state is atomic within one boundary service); there is no `BOOTING → RUNNING`.

content.content:
### 6. Fault codes: static domains, pre-packed constants

A fault code is a positive `int`: `(DOMAIN_ID << 16) | local`, `local` in `1..65535`. **Domain ids are static**, so a code means the same thing in every build, log and fixture. Each system's `*_faults.gd` (a `class_name XFaults extends RefCounted` holding only constants, never instantiated, one class per file) declares `const DOMAIN_ID` and its codes **already packed** (`const NOT_IN_SCOPE: int = (DOMAIN_ID << 16) | 1`), plus `const NAMES: Array[StringName]` indexed by local code. It registers with `register_fault_domain(XFaults.DOMAIN_ID, owner_name, XFaults.NAMES)`; a duplicate or out-of-range id fails boot. A unit test checks each file's constants and `NAMES` agree. Codes are append-only 

**Domain table** (static; new systems take the next free id; ids 32 and up are reserved for VS and later)

| Id | Domain | Id | Domain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | kernel | 8 | interaction |
| 1 | save_load | 9 | suit |
| 2 | content data (item DB, templates, tuning) | 10 | assembly |
| 3 | graph | 11 | web_transit |
| 4 | layout | 12 | attention |
| 5 | body | 13 | horror |
| 6 | emitter | 14 | sanity |
| 7 | controller | 15–31 | presentation and tooling (read-view faults are diagnostics only) |

**Kernel fault codes (domain 0, closed)**

### 9. The kernel state machine is a data table

States: `BOOTING`, `LOADING`, `RUNNING`, `PAUSED`, `SAVING`, `FAULTED`, `SHUTTING_DOWN`. The GDD's transition table is encoded as one constant table `(state, trigger) → target`, where a target may be the sentinel **`PRIOR`** (`SAVING` returns to the state it came from).

- **Triggers** (closed): `request_pause`, `request_resume`, `request_snapshot`, `request_restore`, `request_new_game`, `request_shutdown`, `fault`, `capture_done`, `capture_error`, `load_done`, `load_failed`, `boot_validation_failed`, `teardown_done`.

A runtime fault keeps all three exits.

The control-plane test KRN-STATE-01 is **generated from this table**: every row, every invalid pair, both kinds of `FAULTED`, and the non-transition requests, so a row added without a fixture row fails.

--- L114
**CR-8. State-block registry contract.** An owner registers: `block_id` (unique, namespaced, e.g. `graph.state`); `owner`; `schema_version` (bumped on any serialized-shape change); `class` ∈ {`SIM`, `PERCEPTION_OUT`} (CR-12); The kernel calls each through `Callable.call()` and passes a context object as the last argument (`ApplyContext`/`WriteScope`, `HookContext`, `SnapshotContext`, `NotifyContext`). **Results flow through `ctx`, never through the return value**: `validate(cmd, views, ctx)` reports through `ctx.ok()` or `ctx.reject(reason)`; `snapshot(ctx)`, `default_state(ctx)` and `read_view(ctx)` deliver their payload through `ctx.put(payload)`; `apply(cmd, write_scope, ctx)`, hooks, `restore`, `post_restore`, `init_world`, `commit_baseline`, `snap_baseline` and handlers report only success-by-completion; every callable reports failure with `ctx.fault(code, detail)`. **Every callable's only return statement is `return ctx.complete()`** (a typed token, (b)); no owner callable is declared `-> void`, because a `void` GDScript function cannot return the token and the engine's default for an aborted typed function would alias a legitimate result. A `validate` that calls neither `ok()` nor `reject()` is `Faulted(NO_OUTCOME)`; the first outcome call stands and a second is a violation (`CTX_DOUBLE_OUTCOME`). **Published mutators are not on this list**: other owners, not the kernel, call them, so the kernel cannot check their sentinel; they take the shared `WriteScope`, report with `scope.fault(code, detail)` and return a status that callers propagate — which is also why the sentinel's blind spot (below) is closed by status propagation. The kernel checks `ctx.faulted` (which includes any fault a mutator reported on the shared scope) and the completion token after **every** kernel-invoked call, before using its result. A fault in `apply`, a hook, `snapshot`, `restore`, `post_restore`, `init_world`, `default_state`, `commit_baseline` or `snap_baseline` (and in a mutator they called) moves the kernel to `FAULTED`; **a fault in `read_view` never does**: views are obtained by presentation at render time, outside any tick, and a HUD read must not be able to halt the ship (CR-11, H4) — it is recorded and counted (`INCOMPLETE` or the violation, as a P5 handler's is), the reader receives an empty view, and when sim code called it inside P2/P3 the enclosing `apply` or hook fails through the status it propagates; a fault reported by `validate` does not reject, it faults (a defect), whereas `ctx.reject(reason)` is the ordinary domain rejection (`Rejected(VALIDATION_FAILED(reason))`, kernel stays `RUNNING`); a fault in a P5 or result handler is recorded and counted but cannot fault the kernel (the tick is committed).

lines: **CR-7. Authority model (behaviour).** The host is the sole authority: only a `HOST` kernel ticks and applies; a `MIRROR` never applies. Each command type's owner declares `allowed_origins ⊆ {PLAYER, SYSTEM}` and `actor_binding ∈ {NONE, OWNED_BY_ISSUER}` — both mandatory (CR-6) — and `allowed_origins` is checked at admission, with a P2 re-check as defence in depth. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* A type with `actor_binding = OWNED_BY_ISSUER` also declares **`actor_source`**: the `block_id` of the registered binding source whose ID space its `actor` belongs to (`body.state` for every avatar-acting type, `emitter.state` for `toggle_beam`). The P2 authority check passes iff `(actor_source(type), actor) ∈ half_b[PlayerId(issuer_peer)]`. So an actor and a beam with the same number can never stand in for each other. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* `SYSTEM` commands never arrive from a network; remote ingress always stamps `PLAYER`. The kernel holds a **binding table** — `peer_id → PlayerId` and `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}` — as identity data, not domain state; the table has two halves with different lifetimes *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; Resolved 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling G6 (user delegated all remaining calls): the kernel owns the rebuild; closes Body Open Question 30)*. **(a) `peer_id → PlayerId`** is session state: it is mutated only through a host-only API called by the session owner (`request_bind_seat(peer_id, player_id)` and `request_unbind_seat(peer_id)`, CR-15) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — ADR-0002 GDD sync)* (a boot step in MVP: `HOST_PEER_ID` 1 → PlayerId 1; Co-op Session in VS-B), and a restore, a death restart or a new game never touches it and never resets any issuer's `seq` or `last_seq`. **(b) `PlayerId → {(source block_id, entity_id)}`** *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)* is derived from saved state and is never saved: **the kernel rebuilds it itself as the last step of every pass through `LOADING`** (`request_restore` and `request_new_game` alike), after the last `post_restore()` and the K-4 hash check and before the `LOADING → RUNNING` transition. The rebuild clears half (b) entirely, then calls each registered **binding source** (CR-6, CR-8) in ascending `block_id` order — with `ctx`, as a pure read of its owner's block, under no `WriteScope`, ending `return ctx.complete()` — which delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` in ascending order through `ctx.put`, and binds every pair under the source's own `block_id`: each delivered `(player_id, entity_id)` is stored as `player_id → (source_block_id, entity_id)`. Entity IDs are block-local (CR-8: each owner allocates from its own counter and the kernel allocates none), so the key always carries the source. Equal numbers from two sources (Body actor 1 and Emitter beam 1) are two different keys and never conflict. A key `(source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered for two different PlayerIds, or the same triple `(player_id, source_block_id, entity_id)` delivered twice, is `BINDING_REBUILD_CONFLICT`. A source that reports `ctx.fault` or returns without the sentinel is that source's fault. Either one takes `LOADING → FAULTED` naming the source. The checks compare keys only within one source. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; registry request: `kernel_binding_table` `half_b`, `errors`, `actor_source`, `referenced_by`)* Because `LOADING` is atomic within one boundary service, the rebuild is not a P6 control-plane request and no command can interleave with it; the P6 rule (Section E) governs session-owner changes to half (a) only. At MVP no binding source's pairs change during `RUNNING`, so no `RUNNING` tick sees an empty or stale half (b); a runtime seat or beam reassignment (VS-B) is a session-owner request honoured at P6 (Open Question 4, the co-op ADR). MVP binding sources: Body's `seat_bindings()` (its `SEAT` rows → `(seat, actor_id)`) and the Emitter's `beam_bindings()` (`(player_id, beam_id)`). Single-player: PlayerId 1 → {(`body.state`, avatar actor_id), (`emitter.state`, beam_id)}. Both numbers may be 1 (two independent counters), and the result is valid. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix. Resolved 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix (G6): keyed by source rather than by namespace-tagged IDs, so Body's and the Emitter's persisted ID formats stay unchanged (G1).)* *(Alternative: Player Controller owns the binding as a block — rejected because the kernel could then not authority-check without calling a domain system. → ADR.)* **Single-player is not a special case**: local input is `PLAYER`-origin peer 1 (registry: `HOST_PEER_ID` = 1) acting on an entity peer 1 is bound to; the authority stage runs on every command from day one, so TD-FEASIBILITY's "authority discipline lapsing" risk is structural, not disciplinary. The kernel checks *who*; owners validate *whether the world allows it*; the kernel encodes no game rules. For friendly harm the kernel checks only issuer→actor ownership; the "attacker below the sanity threshold" gate is Interaction's `validate` calling Sanity's query on the actor's authoritative sanity level (a `SIM` block), never on anyone's perception.

-**CR-8. State-block registry contract.** An owner registers: `block_id` (unique, namespaced, e.g. `graph.state`); `owner`; `schema_version` (bumped on any serialized-shape change); `class` ∈ {`SIM`, `PERCEPTION_OUT`} (CR-12); `persist` (false = derived, rebuilt after load) and, when true, `persist_scope` ∈ {`WORLD`, `PROFILE`} — `WORLD` blocks live in the world snapshot and roll back on `request_restore`; `PROFILE` blocks (decoded rules, lore, scars: Pillar 5's "never knowledge") live outside it and are never rolled back by a world restore; `scope` ∈ {`SHARED`, `PER_PLAYER` keyed by PlayerId}; `gameplay` (bool, mandatory: true when a gameplay verb can change the block; false only for settings, menu and save-request state — the CR-16 paused-write test) and `interpolated` (bool, default false: when true the kernel calls the owner's `commit_baseline()` at P4 so the previous/current pair rolls exactly once per tick, and after a restore or an owner-declared teleport/reset the owner calls `snap_baseline(key)` so presentation never interpolates across a discontinuity) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; `repl_hint` ∈ {`HOST_ONLY`, `SHARED_SUMMARY`, `OWNER_PRIVATE`} — mandatory now though unused until VS-B, so no block ever ships without the decision; `snapshot(ctx)` (delivers its plain data through `ctx.put(payload)` and ends with `return ctx.complete()`; canonical state only, deterministic ordering, entity references by stable ID, no derived caches; **the payload is a deep copy** — `duplicate_deep()` for Dictionary/Array, `duplicate()` for Packed arrays, which GDScript passes by reference — never a reference into live state); `restore(data, stored_version, ctx)` (whole-block replace; **copies in** and never retains a reference to `data`, so two restores from one payload cannot alias; the owner migrates from `stored_version`; an unsupported version is a reported failure through the fault channel, never a silent default) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*; `default_state(ctx)` (when a save lacks the block; `ctx.put(state)`); `post_restore(ctx)` (after *all* blocks restore: resolve cross-block IDs, rebuild caches, check invariants); `read_view(ctx)` (the kernel's view-issuing surface calls it and hands the reader `ctx.put(view)`'s content: a getter-only facade or a copy — never a live container, CR-12); `commit_baseline(ctx)` and `snap_baseline(key, ctx)` for `interpolated` blocks; optionally `init_world(world_seed, ctx)` (a new-game step, CR-18); optionally `binding_source(ctx)` (delivers `[(player_id, entity_id)]` ascending through `ctx.put`; read only by the kernel's `LOADING` binding rebuild, CR-7) *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*. **Every one of these is a kernel-invoked owner callable, so every one receives `ctx`, returns only `ctx.complete()`'s token, and is never `-> void`** (CR-19(a)/(b)) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R3)*. Restore order follows declared `restore_after`; a cycle in it, or a reference to an unregistered block, fails boot. *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* Entity IDs are allocated by the owning block from a counter stored inside it; the kernel allocates none. **CR-19. Fault channel, violations and build profiles** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review; replaces the earlier 'throws / asserts' model)*. GDScript has no `try`/`catch`: a runtime script error is printed by the engine, aborts the function it occurred in and hands control back to the caller with a default value the caller cannot distinguish from a result; and `assert()` is compiled out of release exports. The kernel therefore **never relies on an exception or an assertion for control flow**, and every behaviour in this document is identical in debug and release unless a clause calls it a `STRICT_DEBUG` extra.

-- **(a) Fault channel and the one callable contract** *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review, delegated ruling R3; defines the contract once)*. **Kernel-invoked owner callables** are a closed list: `validate`, `apply`, step hooks, `snapshot`, `restore`, `post_restore`, `default_state`, `read_view`, `commit_baseline`, `snap_baseline`, `init_world`, and the result- and subscriber-handlers. The kernel calls each through `Callable.call()` and passes a context object as the last argument (`ApplyContext`/`WriteScope`, `HookContext`, `SnapshotContext`, `NotifyContext`). **Results flow through `ctx`, never through the return value**: `validate(cmd, views, ctx)` reports through `ctx.ok()` or `ctx.reject(reason)`; `snapshot(ctx)`, `default_state(ctx)` and `read_view(ctx)` deliver their payload through `ctx.put(payload)`; `apply(cmd, write_scope, ctx)`, hooks, `restore`, `post_restore`, `init_world`, `commit_baseline`, `snap_baseline` and handlers report only success-by-completion; every callable reports failure with `ctx.fault(code, detail)`. **Every callable's only return statement is `return ctx.complete()`** (a typed token, (b)); no owner callable is declared `-> void`, because a `void` GDScript function cannot return the token and the engine's default for an aborted typed function would alias a legitimate result. A `validate` that calls neither `ok()` nor `reject()` is `Faulted(NO_OUTCOME)`; the first outcome call stands and a second is a violation (`CTX_DOUBLE_OUTCOME`). **Published mutators are not on this list**: other owners, not the kernel, call them, so the kernel cannot check their sentinel; they take the shared `WriteScope`, report with `scope.fault(code, detail)` and return a status that callers propagate — which is also why the sentinel's blind spot (below) is closed by status propagation. The kernel checks `ctx.faulted` (which includes any fault a mutator reported on the shared scope) and the completion token after **every** kernel-invoked call, before using its result. A fault in `apply`, a hook, `snapshot`, `restore`, `post_restore`, `init_world`, `default_state`, `commit_baseline` or `snap_baseline` (and in a mutator they called) moves the kernel to `FAULTED`; **a fault in `read_view` never does**: views are obtained by presentation at render time, outside any tick, and a HUD read must not be able to halt the ship (CR-11, H4) — it is recorded and counted (`INCOMPLETE` or the violation, as a P5 handler's is), the reader receives an empty view, and when sim code called it inside P2/P3 the enclosing `apply` or hook fails through the status it propagates; a fault reported by `validate` does not reject, it faults (a defect), whereas `ctx.reject(reason)` is the ordinary domain rejection (`Rejected(VALIDATION_FAILED(reason))`, kernel stays `RUNNING`); a fault in a P5 or result handler is recorded and counted but cannot fault the kernel (the tick is committed).

-- **(b) Completion sentinel.** The kernel arms `ctx.completed = false` and a fresh `ctx.token` before each call; `ctx.complete()` sets `completed` and returns that token — a typed, non-nil, non-zero object (a per-call `CompletionToken` instance) that the kernel compares **by identity**, so a `null`, `0`, `false` or empty value returned by an aborted or forgetful function can never read as success. A call that returns anything but the armed token with `completed` set (the script aborted on an engine error, or forgot) is `fault(INCOMPLETE)` for `apply`, hooks, `validate`, `snapshot`, `restore`, `post_restore`, `default_state`, `commit_baseline`, `snap_baseline` and `init_world`, and a recorded `INCOMPLETE` diagnostic, without a fault, for a P5 or result handler and for `read_view` (which returns an empty view). In a release build the sentinel is the only abort guard (`assert` is compiled out), so it is exercised on a release export in the spike (Acceptance Criteria, KRN-CTX-06). The sentinel catches a *function that aborted*; it cannot catch an error in a nested helper that the outer function then ignores — which is why mutators also return statuses and callers must propagate them.

I applied the six ADR-0003 GDD sync items. ADR-0003 stays `Proposed`, and nothing is committed. ADR-0003 already existed with this exact scope, so I didn't author a new one. I took the same route you chose for ADR-0001 and ADR-0002 without asking again.

**`design/gdd/command-simulation-layer.md`** (each edit marked "Amended 2026-10-28 — ADR-0003 GDD sync"):
- **CR-19(b):** the completion token is now one per context object, re-armed per call and checked by identity and epoch. Contexts are reused, not allocated per call.
- **CR-8 and CR-19(a):** `read_view` is called once at the registry freeze and returns a long-lived facade. Owners also supply `empty_view`, and `restore` copies into the existing block object. I replaced the old clause about a `read_view` fault inside P2/P3, which no longer applies.
- **CR-18:** `init_world(world_seed, scope, ctx)` receives the shared `INIT` scope. Dirty keys from `INIT` and `RESTORE` scopes are replaced by one `ALL` batch per block on `LOADING → RUNNING`.
- **States and Transitions:** `request_new_game` and `request_restore` from `FAULTED` are legal only when `registry_valid` is true. A boot-failure `FAULTED` exits only to `SHUTTING_DOWN`, which closes OQ-5. Bind and unbind are non-transition requests, `IGNORED` in `FAULTED` and `SHUTTING_DOWN`.
- **Tuning Knobs:**
  - Added a `MAX_SCHEDULE_CYCLE_TICKS` row at 3,600 (range 60–7,200).
  - Added the static fault-domain table, the 17 kernel fault codes and the violation set.
  - Marked `STEP_BUDGET_MS` as an alarm threshold, with the P3 target at 2.0 ms P99.

**`derelict-authoring-handmade-kits.md` and `web-map-and-transit.md`:**
- In derelict, I changed the acceptance criterion to the 2.0 ms P99 target.
- In web-map, I kept `STEP_BUDGET_MS` 4 but labelled it the alarm threshold, because that criterion times individual steps, not the whole P3.

- **Registry:** `MAX_SCHEDULE_CYCLE_TICKS` is not yet in `docs/registry/architecture.yaml`. It needs the usual serial registry pass.
- **Review:** acceptance still waits on the review noted in ADR-0003's Ordering Note.
- **Commit:** the ADR-0001, 0002 and 0003 sync edits together touch seven GDDs plus the three ADR files. Say if you want a commit.

# Architecture Review

The architecture review validates that the complete body of architectural decisions
covers all game design requirements, is internally consistent, and correctly targets
the project's pinned engine version. It is the quality gate between Technical Setup
and Pre-Production.

**Argument modes:**
- **No argument / `full`**: Full review — all phases
- **`coverage`**: Traceability only — which GDD requirements have no ADR
- **`consistency`**: Cross-ADR conflict detection only
- **`engine`**: Engine compatibility audit only
- **`single-gdd [path]`**: Review architecture coverage for one specific GDD
- **`rtm`**: Requirements Traceability Matrix — extends the standard matrix
  to include story file paths and test file paths; outputs
  `docs/architecture/requirements-traceability.md` with the full
  GDD requirement → ADR → Story → Test chain. Use in Production phase when
  stories and tests exist.

---
